ABSTRACT2
High-performance computing (HPC) applications have traditionally relied on parallel file systems3
and file transfer services to manage data movement and storage. Alternative approaches4
have been proposed that use direct communications between application components, trading5
persistence and fault tolerance for speed. Event-driven architectures, as popularized in enterprise6
contexts, present a compelling middle ground, avoiding the performance cost and API constraints7
of parallel file systems while retaining persistence and offering impedance matching between8
application components. However, adapting streaming frameworks to HPC workloads requires9
addressing challenges unique to HPC systems. This paper investigates the potential for a10
streaming framework designed for HPC infrastructures and use cases. We introduce Mofka,11
a persistent event-streaming framework designed specifically for HPC environments. Mofka12
combines the capabilities of a traditional streaming service with optimizations tailored to the13
HPC context, such as support for massively multicore nodes, efficient scaling for large producer-14
consumer workflows, RDMA-enabled high-performance network communications, specialized15
network fabrics with multiple links per node, and efficient handling of large scientific data16
payloads. Built using the Mochi suite of HPC data service components, Mofka provides a17
lightweight, modular, and high-performance solution for persistent streaming in HPC systems.18
We present the architecture of Mofka and evaluate its performance against Kafka and Redpanda19
using benchmarks on diverse platforms, including Argonne’s Polaris and Oak Ridge’s Frontier20
supercomputers, showing up to 8 × improvement in throughput in some scenarios. We21
then demonstrate its utility in several real-world applications: a tomographic reconstruction22
pipeline, a workflow for the discovery of metal-organic frameworks for carbon capture, and the23
instrumentation of Dask workflows for provenance tracking and performance analysis.24
Keywords: HPC, I/O, Streaming, Mochi, Mofka, Kafka, Redpanda25

1 INTRODUCTION
High-performance computing (HPC) applications and workflows are becoming increasingly complex26
as they integrate multimodal data streams from computations, simulations, and/or instruments. Their27
executions require the persistence of data and computing state in the presence of dynamic events such28
as arrival of new measurements and outputs of computing modules. HPC applications have traditionally29
used a parallel file system (PFS) such as Lustre [21] and GPFS [51] to store and manage large amounts of30
scientific data. This approach simplifies use, as it provides a similar file system interface to those used on31
personal computers. The PFS also makes data portable across machines and easy to transfer using common32
file system tools. APIs and libraries such as MPI-IO [19], HDF5 [25], ADIOS [26], and pNetCDF [31]33
provide scalable methods for reading and writing files at scale. However, the PFS approach has limitations34
that researchers have sought to overcome for several decades. The POSIX consistency model forces the use35
of locking or synchronization mechanisms, hindering performance [58]. The need to serialize data into a36
flat file format introduces overheads, and the infamous computation-and-I/O gap causes a performance37
bottleneck at scale [34].38
To overcome these limitations, HPC I/O research has moved in two directions in parallel, beyond simply39
trying to make file I/O more efficient. On the one hand, I/O that requires persistence, such as checkpointing,40
motivated the development of services such as FTI [7] and VeloC [43, 42], which exploit the available41
storage hierarchy (RAM, local SSD, burst buffers, and parallel file systems) and non-blocking I/O and do42
not represent data as files. On the other hand, I/O meant for scientific discovery, carrying data that still43
requires postprocessing, led to in situ analysis approaches [17], which couple analysis and visualization44
software with HPC applications in a way that bypasses the file system altogether.45
Meanwhile, new classes of I/O traffic have emerged. Scientific workflows are becoming more complex and46
more heterogeneous, requiring more elaborate strategies to manage data movement. Tools for provenance47
capture [53], telemetry [1], and anomaly detection [29] produce background I/O traffic from many sources.48
The coupling of supercomputing resources with scientific instruments such as light sources, telescope49
arrays, and gravitational wave detectors introduces new challenges for data management [11]. Machine50
learning and, in particular, federated learning require interactions across facilities [50]. Infrastructures such51
as Globus [15, 16, 64] still make it possible to use the file model, but these new access patterns highlight52
the fact that neither parallel file systems nor current data services, let alone tight-coupling approaches such53
as in situ processing, are a good fit in all cases for HPC data management.54
Complex HPC workflows used to run many scientific applications generate enormous quantities of data55
that can be abstracted as streams of “events” of various types, from small telemetry events to large scientific56
datasets. State-of-the-art distributed event-streaming services such as Kafka [59] and Redpanda [48] show57
how event-driven models can improve scalability by decoupling producers and consumers at scale in58
internet service environments. Achieving comparable impacts in scientific computing. however, requires59
more than simply deploying such services on HPC systems [14]. For example, scientific workloads have60
unique characteristics including large event sizes, specialized data formats, and diverse producer-consumer61
applications, while HPC systems offer high-performance network technologies (e.g., HPE Slingshot,62
Cornelis Omni-Path), communication methods (e.g., RDMA [ 28, 55, 35], and heterogeneous storage63
devices that can significantly improve streaming performance.64
In this paper we explore the potential for an event-driven data management architecture designed65
specifically for HPC. We propose Mofka, a prototype of such a streaming framework, developed using66
the Mochi suite of components for HPC data services [49]. Mofka natively leverages HPC networks and67

The second contribution of this paper is the presentation of three use cases where an event-driven approach,72

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents motivation for using persistent streaming77
systems in an HPC context by drawing a parallel with their use in businesses. Section 3 introduces Mofka.78
Section 4 evaluates Mofka on multiple machines and compares its performance with that of Kafka and79

2 MOTIVATION: EVENT-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES
The event-driven architecture is presented as a solution to these problems. A distributed, persistent, resilient83
event-streaming system is set up as the single source of truth and as the means for departments/applications84
to communicate, with each having a set of topics it produces information to or consumes from. A schema85
is still required for applications to understand each other, but these schemas are managed by a schema86
registry, making it easy for changes to be picked up automatically. A fault in an application no longer87
affects other applications, because the faulty application will simply restart and pick up where it left off in88
the stream of events it subscribed to.89
Much as exploratory data analysis (EDA) solves data management challenges in large businesses,90
we argue that it could also overcome most of the challenges posed by existing HPC data management91
approaches such as parallel file systems, data services, and in situ processing. HPC applications are natural92
producers and consumers of immutable data. They do not need file consistency semantics, and they do not93
need file formats (in situ analysis is an evidence of that fact). EDA brings back persistence, resilience, and94
impedance matching, which are missing from the in situ approach. It naturally reconciles offline and inline95
processing and has the potential for being the backbone of complex workflows. EDA is also well suited to96
the needs of emerging HPC workflows, including provenance capture, anomaly detection, communications97
with scientific instruments, and cross-facility interactions.98
Event-streaming software such as Kafka [59] and Redpanda [48] provide an EDA solution for businesses.99
Cloud providers such as AWS and Confluent provide cloud-managed Kafka deployments. Azure Event Hubs100
accept the Kafka protocol. However, these software products have been developed for cloud environments101
(whether public or private). They do not make use of features specific to HPC systems such as massively102
multicore nodes, high-performance networks, remote direct memory access (RDMA), and multiple NICs;103
and they do not cater to application spanning hundreds of thousands of processes. In the following, we104
introduce Mofka, an event-streaming service specifically designed for HPC use cases.105

3 THE MOFKA EVENT-STREAMING FRAMEWORK
While heavily inspired by the likes of Apache Kafka, Mofka aims to better support HPC application by108
leveraging the hardware available on high-end supercomputers. This section starts by listing design goals,109
before diving into Mofka’s architecture, its API, and its implementation.110
3.1 Design goals111
For Mofka to be suitable for an HPC context, we designed it with the following goals in mind.112
1. Efficient network usage. HPC machines rely on high-performance networks such as Infiniband,113
Omni-Path, or Slingshot. While the TCP stack is available on top of these networks, it is not the best114
transport to maximize throughput and minimize latency. Instead, an event-driven system for HPC115
should natively use the high-performance transport, including RDMA capabilities, to transfer data116
directly from the application’s memory to the target storage device with as few data copies as possible117
and as little kernel and CPU involvement as possible. Furthermore, we start to find compute nodes118
with multiple NICs. Argonne’s Polaris features two NICs per node, and Aurora features eight. Making119
efficient use of all the NICs is also critical.120
2. Efficient threading. Compute nodes on HPC machines feature an increasingly larger number of cores.121
Hence, an event-driven system may be used concurrently by a large number of threads or processes.122
Such a large number of cores is also an opportunity for the event-driven system to offload tasks such as123
serialization, validation, and batching. An event-driven system for HPC should make efficient use of124
this multicore environment.125
3. Handling of large data. Event-driven systems in enterprises are typically used for small, structured126
messages. In an HPC context, users may want to attach large payloads (multiple megabytes to multiple127
gigabytes) to each event. An event-driven system for HPC should be able to handle a wider range of128
event sizes than traditional event-driven systems can handle.129
4. Support for scientific data. HPC applications usually produce multidimensional arrays of numerical130
data. Consumers of such data may be interested in only some sections of such arrays. An event-driven131
system for HPC should allow consumers to specify such interest before the event is transferred, in132
order to improve transfer speeds.133
5. High modularity. An event-driven system for HPC should adapt to vastly different supercomputer134
hardware and application workloads. This calls for a modular design where everything from the135
network stack, to internal scheduling policies, or to local storage usage can be changed and fine-tuned136
for each individual use case.137
These design goals led to the architecture and implementation described hereafter.138

Figure 1 shows the Mofka architecture. A key difference between Mofka and other streaming services152
such as Kafka is that Mofka divides events into two parts: a metadata part, which is assumed to be small153
and structured, that is, interpretable by both clients and servers (such as a JSON document), and a data154
part, which can be much larger and would carry a scientific payload that is opaque to the server.155
This division matches typical HPC use cases where large amounts of data may need to be transferred and156
persisted together with some metadata describing it. For example, in a distributed deep-learning application,157
the data part could contain an update to apply to a particular layer of a deep neural network, in the form158
of a list of tensors, while the metadata could contain information on how this update was produced, for159
provenance tracing. In a workflow coupling a light source with a supercomputer, the data could be an X-ray160
diffraction image, and the metadata could contain the settings used by the sensors and information about161
the sample being scanned.162
This division of metadata and data allows Mofka to use different tools to transfer the two parts and163
independently optimize the control and data path in order to minimize overhead. Metadata parts are164
serialized into batches that are sent via RDMA to an intermediate buffer in the server, before making their165
way to a “log provider.” Data parts, on the other hand, are transferred by using RDMA directly to and from166
user-provided memory and to and from their final storage destination. Structuring it in such a way helps167
avoid serialization overhead, reduce memory overhead, and leverage direct RDMA transfers for the highest168
volume portion of each event.169

3.2.1 Producing events170
Producer applications (on the left of Figure 1) interact with the service via a topic handle. This handle171
contains a validator, a partition selector, and a serializer: three user-provided objects that work on an172
event’s metadata before it makes its way into a batch. The validator checks that the metadata satisfies a173
particular format expected for the topic (for instance, that it is valid JSON or that this JSON satisfies a174
particular schema). The partition selector decides which partition a particular event will be sent to. It can175
do so based on the metadata content or based on any algorithm (e.g., random, round-robin). The serializer176
takes the metadata and writes it into a batch. As an example, the validator could check that the metadata is a177
valid JSON object with a floating point “energy” attribute (e.g., {"energy": 123.456 }); the partition178
selector could decide on the target partition based on this energy value, and the serializer could simply179
write the 8-byte double value rather than the full JSON string.180
Once a batch is formed, it is sent to a partition manager, the component in charge of a single partition in181
a server. This partition manager redirects the batch of metadata to a log provider and the RDMA handles182
for the data to a storage provider. It then creates the association between each metadata and each data part183
and adds it to the log provider.184
Similar to the concept of schema registry in event-driven systems, the validator, partition selector, and185
serializer are provided when creating a topic and are stored in a master database in Mofka. This ensures186
that all producer and consumer applications use the same objects for a given topic.187
3.2.2 Mofka servers188
Mofka itself consists of a set of server processes running the components shown in Figure 1. As we will189
show in Section 3.3, the user has full control over where these components live, where each partition is190
located, and how it is implemented.191
One partition manager handles a single partition of a single topic; hence, creating a topic and its partitions192
means instantiating the necessary number of partition managers across multiple processes.193
Mofka partition managers keep track of which consumer is subscribed to them and actively fetch batches194
of metadata from the log provider to send to the consumer. However, it does not proactively send them the195
data part of each event, as will be explained next.196
3.2.3 Consuming events197
Consumer applications (right part of the picture) also interact with Mofka using a topic handle, by198
subscribing to a given set of partitions from the topic. The topic’s serializer, retrieved from the master199
database, allows deserializing the metadata part of the received events.200
Mofka consumers must be initialized with user-provided data selector and data broker objects. A Mofka201
partition manager only sends the metadata part of events, in batches. Upon receiving and deserializing202
them, the consumer invokes its data selector to decide which part of the data (all, none, or any arbitrary203
subset) it is interested in. This is another place where the division of events into a metadata part and a204
data part allows transfer optimizations, since the consumer application can decide to transfer only a subset205
of the data part. This also means that multiple consumers could consume from the same topic but with a206
focus on different parts of the data. As an example, in a weather application where events contain a 3D207
“chunk” of atmosphere, a consumer may be selecting a 2D slice at ground level to display a color map,208
while another consumer could pull the full data for volume rendering.209

3.5 A Parallel file system turned inside out258
Distributed streaming frameworks such as Apache Kafka are often described as “a database turned inside259
out” because they invert the conventional architecture of data-centric systems. Traditional databases260
prioritize storage and subsequent querying of data, typically treating the change log as an internal261
implementation detail. In contrast, Kafka exposes the append-only commit log as a first-class abstraction,262
positioning it as the central system of record. Data is ingested as an immutable, ordered sequence of events,263
which can be consumed, processed, and replayed by multiple downstream systems. This design enables264
decoupled, real-time data processing pipelines and supports scalable, event-driven architectures that are265
fundamentally more transparent and flexible than traditional database systems.266
In this sense, Mofka be viewed as a “parallel file system turned inside out.” Traditional parallel file267
systems require users to reason carefully about data layout within files to achieve acceptable performance,268
often entangling application logic with low-level storage considerations. Mofka inverts this paradigm269
by replacing file-based I/O with persistent, ordered streams of events, allowing users to focus on the270
semantics of data production and consumption rather than its physical organization on disk. By decoupling271
data movement from file management, Mofka enables applications to exchange data efficiently and272
asynchronously across distributed nodes, without sacrificing durability or throughput. This abstraction273
simplifies the development of real-time, event-driven workflows in HPC systems, aligning with the need274
for low-latency communication and scalable I/O in modern scientific applications.275

4.2 Benchmark design297
Properly benchmarking messaging systems is difficult. Although the Open Messaging Benchmark13 is,298
to the best of our knowledge, the only open-source benchmark available to evaluate the performance of299
messaging systems, this benchmark is no longer maintained and is not adapted to the deployment of many300
producers and consumers as MPI jobs on a supercomputer. Hence, we had to design our own benchmark.301
Our benchmark is written in C++ for two reasons. The first is to avoid any language binding overheads;302
the second is to streamline integration with librdkafka.303
We are interested in aggregate throughput from a large number of producers or consumers. Hence our304
benchmark consists of an MPI application that starts N client processes on multiple cores of multiple305
nodes. This setup is representative of how HPC applications would use Mofka or any event-driven system.306
In producer mode, each process produces a desired number of messages of a specified size to a designated307
partition. We rely on a fixed assignment of producer to partition to avoid variations in performance caused308
by unbalanced load. While cloud-computing applications are more elastic, HPC workloads generally309
execute in fixed-size job, where the number of clients is known in advance.310
In all our experiments we produce and consume 10 million events per partition. The messages are311
produced in batches of 1,000 messages for Mofka, and we let librkafka manage its own batching (librdkafka312
producers batch messages automatically and send the batches from a background thread). A flush313
operation is invoked every 10,000 events. One million events are produced as a warmup before we start314
measuring performance. In consumer mode, each process consumes messages from a specific partition,315
again with a fixed assignment to avoid the overhead of rebalancing operations. We consume events in316
batches of 1,000 events. We therefore consume in batches of 1,000 events both with Mofka and with317
librdkafka.318

4.3 Tuning considerations319
Mofka, Kafka, and Redpanda are complex systems with many tuning parameters that can dramatically320
affect performance. Months of evaluating them and exchanging with the developers and users of Kafka and321
Redpanda led us to what we believe is the best performance we could achieve for each of these systems.322
For Kafka for example, our investigations included varying the number of I/O threads and network threads.323
Redpanda requires root permissions to tune kernel parameters, which we cannot do on production HPC324
systems. We therefore warn the reader that better performance may be achievable from Redpanda if set up325
by a system administrator with escalated privileges.326
Lesson 1: Configuration parameters are highly sensitive.
Our experiments taught us that slight changes to configuration parameters or to the client code can
have a significant impact on performance. We advise authors of any future studies on such systems,
as well as any users and practitioners, to spend enough time investigating these aspects.

4.7 Benchmarking conclusions418
The conclusion from our benchmarking campaign (of which the above is only a representative subset)419
is that relying on HPC technologies such as RDMA and native high-performance networks often leads420
to better performance than using systems designed for a cloud environment. However, many factors also421
impact performance before the network even starts to play its part. Such factors include the number of422
processes in the application, the API used, the threading technique, process and thread placement (including423
oversubscription), and SSD speed.424
A caveat not shown in the figures above is that the Kafka and Redpanda systems frequently timed out and425
failed to complete benchmarks as we increased concurrency. Considerable effort was needed to identify426
configuration permutations that would avoid this issue. This would make them difficult to use in an HPC427
environment without careful engagement from an experienced administrator. We believe that librdkafka428
was the common root cause of many of these issues for both systems, but we found it difficult to get429
community support for our particular problems.430
Lesson 8: We should invest more in developing an HPC-ready event-driven system.
Comparing Mofka with Kafka (or Redpanda) for event streaming is like comparing Lustre with NFS:
the former is HPC-ready, uses high-performance networks, and offers the right set of features for
file I/O in HPC applications. The latter is useful in an HPC context; and while the modern NFSv4
has made progress in handling parallel I/O, it will always rely on Ethernet and have performance
limitations for HPC applications. Kafka’s development started in 2011 and Redpanda’s in 2019; each
is production software backed by a company and used by large businesses. The fact that we were
able, with limited resources and in a short time, to develop a competing prototype for the HPC space
that outperforms them in many scenarios is an encouraging first step that we think justifies more
investments in this direction.

TekApp comprises four components: (1)) data acquisition (DAQ), (2)) distribution (DIST), (3)458

5.1.7 Lessons Learned from TekApp601
Lesson 10: Batch size matters.
The batch size can have an important impact on throughput when producing and consuming events,
especially when producing small events. However, a large batch size is not necessarily better,
since it may delay production and consumption, increase latency, and prevent properly overlapping
computation with data transfers.
602
Lesson 11: Don’t batch large events.
Mofka separates the metadata and data part of an event so more efficient RDMA techniques can
be used for the data part. When this data part is large, there is little benefit to batching more events
together because the performance will be driven by the transfer of the data part, rather than the
number of RPCs issued.
603
Lesson 12: Python binding has an overhead.
Some of the components in TekApp are written in Python. Not shown in our experiments above, but
observed during our experiments using HPCToolkit, is the fact that Python can incur an important
performance overhead. The conversion of a large number of Python objects to C++ and vice versa can
often have more impact than the serialization of events or their transfer. Furthermore, Python’s Global
Interpreter Lock (GIL) makes it difficult to enable concurrency, especially in Mofka consumers,
where Python-based data selectors and data brokers need to be invoked.
604
Lesson 13: More partitions equals more parallelism.
Increasing the number of partitions, even to produce (or consume) from a single process to a single
server, allows for more parallelism and better performance.

Events flowing through Colmena queues are JSON objects of varying sizes. Many control and metadata629

5.2.1 How Mofka transforms MOFA639
In the original MOFA implementation, all task coordination and data exchange were handled through a640
single Redis instance co-located with the Colmena Thinker process on the login node. This Redis-backed641
queuing model introduced two critical limitations: it created a single point of failure, where a crash or stall642
in Redis could leave the workflow in an unrecoverable state, and it constrained throughput when event rates643
are high, as all data and control traffic were funneled through a single login node.644
To address these challenges, we replaced Redis-based Colmena queues with Mofka-backed queues,645
leveraging Mofka’s distributed, persistent event-streaming architecture. As in the original setup, each646
task type publishes results to a dedicated queue, now mapped to a Mofka topic, while task requests are647
consolidated into a shared request topic. Unlike Redis, however, Mofka topics are distributed across a648
cluster of brokers, allowing the workflow to scale more effectively and recover gracefully from failures.649

Neon [38] was a first take on streaming for HPC in the context of the Mochi framework. While not819

Chronolog [30] was proposed to handle logs from very large HPC applications, emphasizing the need to822

6.2 Producer/consumer HPC services843
As stated in Section 1, HPC applications are fundamentally producers and consumers of data, rather844
than modifiers. Scientific simulations produce periodic outputs that must be consumed by analysis and845
visualization tools. Scientific instruments are producers of sensor data that must be sent to post-processing846
tools on supercomputers. HPC workflows comprise tasks that produce and consume data. If a file needs to847
be modified, it is generally to update a header or metadata related to its structure, not to touch its scientific848
content. Hence, most HPC data services can be thought of as addressing this producer/consumer pattern.849
ADIOS [26], initially developed as an I/O library with modular backend plugins, provides the SST plugin850
for streaming [23]. SST is not a data service, in the sense that it does not require extra servers running851
a specific software. Rather, it turns the producing application into a data service. Put operations queue852
application data locally, making it remotely available to the consumer application’s Get operations via853
RDMA. SST does not provide persistence. However, it illustrates the need for efficient streaming in HPC854
applications.855
Checkpointing systems are also frequently used together with producer/consumer patterns. They facilitate856
a decoupled interaction between producers and consumers by enabling the capture and reuse of key data857
structures. Multilevel checkpointing solutions such as VeloC [ 43, 42] leverage both node-local (GPU858
memory, host memory, NVMe) and remote storage to cache and persist checkpoints asynchronously, which859
reduces the I/O overheads significantly by masking them in the background. These techniques can be860
combined with prefetching to co-optimize checkpointing initiated by the producers with the reuse patterns861
of the consumers, which can be especially effective if the consumers express their intent (hints about what862
checkpoints to read in what order) in advance [39]. The convenience of working with decoupled checkpoint863
files also can be leveraged at the system level by intercepting I/O calls and transparently implementing864
them as direct links between producers and consumers. This was demonstrated by LowFive [46] for the865
popular HDF5 [24] format, with notable applications for AI workflows that need to continuously train866
learning models (producers) that need to be used at the same time for inferences (consumers) [63].867

Originally meant as a message queuing system, Apache Pulsar [52] is an alternative to Kafka that later892
added event-streaming capabilities. Contrary to the monolithic design of Kafka, Pulsar decouples message893

KerA [36] is similar to Kafka but proposes a hierarchical partitioning of the data, splitting topics into a898

7 CONCLUSION
Event-driven systems have been massively adopted in internet businesses to provide a single source of truth909
while decoupling applications. In HPC, such a model could be adopted just as well to support workflows910
made of applications that produce and consume data.911
In this paper we investigated the potential for an event-driven framework tailored to HPC systems912
by exemplifying three such workflows. While exceptions exist (e.g., AI-training applications requiring913
random accesses to a large number of sample data), many HPC applications can be thought of as a914
producer/consumer workflow. Traditional, bulk-synchronous scientific simulations are periodic producers915
of checkpoints, for which postprocessing tools are their consumers. With the emergence of more complex916
workflows, a distributed, persistent, event-driven framework for HPC becomes increasingly relevant,917
enabling decoupling workflow components and impedence matching between production and consumption918
rates.919
Our Mofka framework, based on the Mochi suite of components for HPC data services, makes use of HPC920
technologies such as high-speed networks with RDMA and efficient multithreading to efficiently support921
HPC applications. In this study we showed that (1) there is an advantage to relying on such HPC-specific922
technology to design an event-driven system for HPC, rather than relying on technologies from the cloud923
computing and internet landscape, as motivated by performance evaluation comparing Mofka with Kafka924
and Redpanda, and (2) there is an actual need for such an event-driven system in HPC, as exemplified by925
three workflows in which Mofka is now used.926
As future work, we plan to make Mofka resilient by enabling data replication as done in Kafka and927
Redpanda. We will do so using a custom, RDMA-enabled implementation of the RAFT protocol. We also928
plan to turn Mofka into a multiuser service by enabling authentication and access control, using MUNGE,18929
OpenSSL,19 and a methodology we recently released for developing multiuser Mochi-based services.20930
We also plan to explore bridging Mofka with other technologies such as Octopus [45] to make it part of931
a larger, scientific event fabric. In this context Mofka would form the HPC part of such an event fabric932
